question: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In January 2025, the Centre for Research on Multinational Corporations (SOMO) published a report1 documenting how JBS, one of the world’s largest meat companies, allegedly used Luxembourg-based mailbox subsidiaries and intra-group arrangements to substantially reduce its tax liabilities. Between 2019 and 2022, JBS may have avoided approximately USD 293 million in corporate income taxes and USD 148 million in withholding taxes, relying on entities with little or no economic substance. Given that one year has passed since the publication of this report, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it has formally assessed the evidence presented by SOMO and engaged with the Luxembourg authorities regarding these structures?
Whether any inquiries, investigations or corrective actions have been initiated in response to these findings?

What concrete measures it plans to adopt to curb the use of mailbox companies and aggressive tax planning within the EU, including stronger rules on withholding taxes and the prevention of mismatches between national tax systems?
Ensuring that multinational companies pay their fair share of tax is essential for public finances, fair competition and the credibility of the EU’s tax agenda.
https://www.somo.nl/jbss-global-tax-avoidance-hub-luxembourg/
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) Compliance with tax rules falls under the responsibility of the country which adopted such rules. The Commission remains fully committed to tackling cross-border tax avoidance and evasion as well as aggressive tax planning at international level. The EU has strong tools to counteract tax avoidance practices (notably the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive1). The Pillar Two Directive2, set out rules to ensure a minimum effective level of taxation for large multinational groups in every jurisdiction where they operate; this is applicable since 31 December 2023. With regard to Luxembourg, the Commission also introduced countryspecific recommendations on aggressive tax planning as of 2019. The 2025 country-specific recommendations on aggressive tax planning notably target the risks that arise from aggressive tax planning opportunities in the absence of sound defensive measures on outbound payments – especially interest and royalty payments – towards jurisdictions with zero or very low taxation. The Commission attaches great importance to maintaining an open and constructive dialogue with the European Parliament on these critical issues.
1 Council Directive (EU) 2016/1164 of 12 July 2016 laying down rules against tax avoidance practices that

directly affect the functioning of the internal market. 2 Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 of 14 December 2022 on ensuring a global minimum level of taxation for multinational enterprise groups and large-scale domestic groups in the Union.
